newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Chechnya to speed up long-term peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Chechnya to speed up long-term peace deal.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin and Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov said on Monday they wanted to speed up a long-term settlement between Russia and its rebel region but appeared at odds over the terms of the possible deal.

Maskhadov emerged upbeat after talks with Yeltsin, saying he had high hopes of negotiating formal independence for Chechnya, but Yeltsin's comments left little impression that Moscow was ready to accept secession.
"We are pressing today for the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria to be recognised as an independent sovereign state," Maskhadov told a news conference after talks. "In what form, time will tell."
"During this lengthy discussion between two presidents, both came to the common opinion that we must take this step."

Yeltsin sounded equally committed to reaching a long-term solution to the Chechen problem, which erupted into a 21-month war when Russia sent troops in December 1994 to subdue the region's three-year independence bid.

The war ended in a shaky peace deal last August under which Russia withdrew its forces from Chechnya in exchange for a promise by separatist leaders to put off a decision on Chechnya's future status until 2001.
Yeltsin cautiously avoided any mention of independence, making clear he was prepared to talk with Maskhadov, but only on the same terms as other Russian regional leaders.

"We will solve the problems as we did with Shaimiyev," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying in a reference to a power-sharing deal with Tatarstan leader Mentimer Shaimiyev which helped the Kremlin in 1994 to head off confrontation with another independent-minded province on the Volga River.
Russia's chief negotiator with Chechnya, Ivan Rybkin, said that special four-man groups from each would start the search for a mutually acceptable formula of future relations.

Rybkin, who is also the secretary of Yeltsin's policy-making Security Council, hinted that Moscow was ready to consider most options for Chechnya as long as they did not look like an outright secession.

"There may be all sorts of statuses for members of the Russian federation, there may be different sorts of enclaves and such," he told a separate news conference. "In any case I deeply believe that Russia's territorial integrity will not be harmed."
"Chechnya wants to take over most (government) functions. No one would mind this," he said. "The key point on which we agreed is preserving a single defence, economy and finances."
Rybkin shrugged off Maskhadov's earlier proposals to establish diplomatic relations between Russia and Chechnya. "We have far warmer relations than diplomatic," he said.

Rybkin said that Yeltsin also urged Maskhadov to free Russians and a number of foreigners still being held in Chechnya and make efforts to clamp down on banditry, which has flourished in the southern province for years.

Udugov said on Sunday that two journalists from a private Russian television company, seized on June 11, had been freed on the eve of the talks. The NTV commercial channel said on Monday that three of its journalists, seized more than three months ago, had also been released.
Two Britons, five French people, a German, a Slovak and a Yugoslav are among those currently missing in Chechnya.
Rybkin has said the number of people still missing, including captives taken during the war, totals 1,407.
